finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so the dba role check is never enforced. Any request that reaches the handler with a user in context can run the DROP TABLE.
finding.source: Any caller who can reach POST/GET /admin/drop on :8083 with any user in the request context (no dba role needed).
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27, a destructive admin operation.

trace.note: /admin/drop registered on the default mux, listening on :8083 (all interfaces) at line 46
userFrom(r) obtains the user from the context
Authorize(u, "dba") return value is discarded, so a forbidden result does not stop execution
execution continues to runSQL with the attacker-controlled table name

finding.guards_checked: Compared with vacuum (api.go:33-36), which checks the error and returns 403. dropTable has no early return. No auth middleware is registered in main. userFrom is a bare type assertion, so a missing user would panic and net/http would recover it, but any request that has some user is not blocked.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u,"dba") at api.go:26 is called but its error is discarded, so it has no effect. No middleware exists. userFrom (api.go:22) panics if no user is in context, and nothing in this code sets one.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 discards the error from Authorize, so any request with a non-dba user in context reaches runSQL("DROP TABLE "+r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27, unlike vacuum at api.go:33-36, which returns 403.

finding.claim: SQL injection: the form parameter t is concatenated directly into a DROP TABLE statement without validation or an identifier allowlist.
finding.source: r.FormValue("t"), a query-string or form body parameter on /admin/drop.

trace.note: dropTable handler receives the HTTP request
r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into the SQL string and passed to runSQL
runSQL is a stub that does nothing. The injection is real in the pattern but not demonstrable here, and a real implementation would execute the string.

finding.guards_checked: No sanitization, quoting or table-name allowlist. DROP TABLE cannot be parameterized, so an identifier allowlist is needed. The only guard is the dba check, which is bypassed by AUTH-1. The impact depends on how runSQL is implemented, since the stub is empty.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the result is discarded as a bare statement, so it never blocks. There is no allowlist, quoting or parameterization on the table name. The sibling vacuum handler at api.go:33 does check the error, which confirms the check was intended.
verdict.reason: api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into "DROP TABLE " with no identifier allowlist, and the only guard, Authorize at api.go:26, has its error ignored, so any user who passes the user-context lookup at api.go:22 can reach it. The sink runSQL is an empty stub at api.go:41, so the real impact depends on the production implementation.

finding.claim: userFrom does an unchecked type assertion on the context value. If no upstream authentication middleware set the "user" key, the assertion panics. No authentication middleware exists in this code, so the user identity source is unverified.
finding.source: An unauthenticated request to any /admin/* route.
finding.sink: r.Context().Value("user").(*User) at api.go:22, followed by the role checks.

trace.note: /admin/drop and /admin/vacuum are registered on the default mux with no auth middleware
the bare assertion panics on a nil value, and net/http recovers the panic per request

finding.guards_checked: Looked for authentication middleware or context population in this repository and found none. It may be supplied elsewhere, which would make this a robustness issue (a panic instead of a 401) rather than a bypass. Low confidence.

verdict.guard_found: None for authentication. Nothing in the repo sets the "user" context key, so the bare assertion at api.go:22 panics before any handler logic or SQL runs. net/http recovers the panic per request, so the server stays up.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (api.go:44 registers the routes without middleware, and api.go:22 does the bare assertion). But an unauthenticated request panics inside userFrom at api.go:25/32, before runSQL at api.go:27/37. The request fails closed and net/http recovers, so this is a robustness issue (a 500 or dropped connection instead of a 401), not an auth bypass or a DoS. The separate bug at api.go:26, where the Authorize result is discarded, is not this finding and is only reachable if a user value is somehow set.
